tagline.text: A Neo-Gothic national cultural treasure in western Bohol modeled on Manila's Santo Domingo Church

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Calape, western Bohol, about 42 km north of Tagbilaran

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (half a day as part of a western Bohol itinerary)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, based on a round-trip day trip from Tagbilaran by public transport including meals)

children.text: Calape Church is the parish church dedicated to Saint Vincent Ferrer, a Neo-Gothic building begun in 1933 and completed in 1954. It was damaged in the 2013 earthquake, restored in 2019 and declared a National Cultural Treasure in May 2023.
Calape is a town on the western coast of Bohol facing the Cebu Strait, about
42 km

north of Tagbilaran. It borders Loon to the west and Tubigon to the east, so you meet it along the road between Tagbilaran and Tubigon, the gateway port for boats from Cebu. The town's name is said to come from kalapi, a rattan that was once abundant here, and another account says it meant a gathering place for traders and fishermen. It is reported that the governor of Cebu established it as an independent municipality in 1802, and a native settlement existed before that. Eighteen of its 33 barangays face the sea, and the 2024 census counted about 33,000 residents. Most of the coast is a fairly level plain, and inland it rises into gently rolling coralline limestone hills. The Tultugan and Liboron rivers flow into Calape Bay, and the Calunasan and Abucayan Norte rivers flow into Tipcan Bay. In 1957 the barangays of Abucayan Norte and Abucayan Sur were created, among other changes as the town grew, and about 92 percent of residents are Roman Catholic, so the church still plays a central role in daily life.
The first place travelers look for here is the
Parish Church of Saint Vincent Ferrer

. The parish was founded in 1802, the year the town was established, and was first run by Augustinian Recollect missionaries before passing to secular priests in 1898. The first church was a modest building with a stone foundation, a nipa palm roof and walls of lime-and-sand-coated bamboo or hardwood slats. The present stone church was begun in 1933 and completed in 1954, with Eliseo Josol and Rosalio Real leading construction. The design is said to be based on Santo Domingo Church in Intramuros, Manila. A bell cast in 1690 is reportedly hung in the belfry, so while the building is from the 20th century, the sound is much older.

Look closely at the architecture. The church uses pointed Gothic arches throughout, and the entrance is a colonnaded portico with white interlacing relief arches. The façade is divided into three vertical panels by pilasters, and the upper level has three pointed arches framing two rectangular glass windows, a quatrefoil and relief decoration. At the top is a pointed-arch pediment with crockets and a rose opening, and the two flanking belfries also have crocketed pinnacles, rose windows, paired arched openings with balustrades and pyramidal roofs. On the ground level are three blind arches, the middle one holding the entrance, with a statue of the patron saint above it. Where the other Spanish-era coral-stone churches of Bohol are Baroque in feeling, this one has a different mood, given by its Gothic spires. Standing in front, the façade and towers are symmetrical, and the impression changes between a view from afar and a view up close. We suggest first looking at the overall outline from across the plaza, then standing between the columns under the portico and looking up at the layered arches.

The church was damaged by the magnitude 7.2 Bohol earthquake of October 2013 and was restored in 2019. On May 9, 2023, the National Museum of the Philippines declared it a National Cultural Treasure. It did not collapse completely like neighboring Loon Church, but it is meaningful to see a building that was shaken by the earthquake open and in use again. Because Calape is a coastal town, it is better to fit the church into a half-day trip along the western coast road together with Loon Church and the port of Tubigon than to come only for the church. Since the parish church is still in use, interior viewing may not be possible during Mass and events, so check before you visit. If you want to see Bohol's earthquake-restored churches in one go, going up the northern coast road from Tagbilaran in the order Maribojoc, Loon, Calape makes for natural travel. Each church differs in size and style, so comparing them is part of the fun.

The façade is divided into three vertical panels, with a belfry on each side. The rose opening above the pointed pediment and the crocketed pinnacles are delicate up close. The best times to see the exterior are the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low.

blocks.title: Colonnaded portico and patron saint statue

children.text: A statue of Saint Vincent Ferrer stands above the main entrance, and the portico is a colonnade of interlaced white arches. The capitals and bases are clearly distinct, which makes it good for photos.

A bell cast in 1690 is said to hang in the belfry. The building dates from the 20th century but the bell is described as much older. You can hear it at Mass times, so plan your visit around them. Ask locally whether you can go up the bell tower, and do not climb without permission.
The National Museum of the Philippines declared it so on
. Since the declaration the building can receive restoration and conservation support, so check whether there is an information marker in the church grounds.

The church is in the Poblacion, close to the town's market and offices. The area around the plaza lets you see everyday local life and snacks, and is good for a short walk. Shops selling handicrafts and local snacks are reported at the market, so you can browse for souvenirs.

Calape faces the Cebu Strait and Calape Bay, and most of its coast is fairly level. After seeing the church you can walk along the shore and look across the strait toward Cebu. The town's average temperature is about
and annual rainfall is reported at about 1,326 mm. It is a good place to rest with a snack and enjoy the coastal-town atmosphere.

Calape includes Pangangan Island (eight barangays) and Mantatao Island, and also the uninhabited islets of Poom and Basihan. Check boats and safety locally before deciding to visit an island. Mantatao had a population of about 849 in the 2024 census, so it is a small and quiet island village. Any island may lack lodging and facilities, so on a day trip check the return boat time first.

Seeing the church and the Inang-angan stairway of neighboring Loon to the west on the same day completes a western Bohol heritage itinerary. The two towns are close by road, so you can reverse the order.
Take a bus or van bound for Tubigon from the Dao terminal in Tagbilaran.
Get off at Loon and see Loon Church and the Inang-angan stairway first.
Have lunch and head toward Calape.
Look around the façade, the bell tower and the portico of Calape Church.
If Mass is not in progress, quietly look inside.
Walk around the plaza and the shore, then head to Tagbilaran or Tubigon.
Bus times change, so check the last return departure in advance.
Arrive at Tubigon by boat from Cebu and see Calape Church first.
Pass through Loon and continue toward Tagbilaran and your hotel.
Flights run from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG) and take about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Check airlines and schedules when you book.
From the airport to Tagbilaran takes about
30 minutes
by taxi or van.
From the Dao terminal in Tagbilaran, take a bus or van bound for Tubigon and get off at Calape. The distance is about
42 km
, and the time depends on traffic, so allow around an hour.

Ordinary bus fares are reported at roughly ₱80~170 (2026 aggregator figures that vary widely by source; air-conditioned buses add ₱15~25). Southern Star buses reportedly run hourly, so confirm the exact fare at the terminal.
Ferries run from Cebu to Tubigon port, which neighbors Calape. Ferry schedules and fares differ by operator, so check when you book.
A private car or chartered van makes it easy to connect Loon, Calape and Tubigon along the western coastal highway.
Within town, use a tricycle.
Calape's average temperature is about
, and annual rainfall is reported at about 1,326 mm with about 259 rainy days. Because the trip centers on buildings, the dry season with less rain is easier.
During church events and Holy Week, Masses run long and interior viewing may be difficult, so we recommend a weekday afternoon for a quiet visit.

Calape is a small town without many lodgings, so travelers usually stay in Tagbilaran or Panglao and come as a day trip. Near the port of Tubigon there is lodging for port users, so look there if your trip passes through Cebu. Book early during event periods such as Holy Week.

Food centers on restaurants and the market in town. Being a coastal town it has seafood and simple local eateries, but we could not confirm specific restaurants, so choose on site. It is convenient to have lunch in town before or after visiting the church. Calape is a 2nd-class municipality by income class, with about 7,900 households, so it is a small-to-mid-sized town. It is not a major tourist destination, so shops cater mainly to local residents and some may close in the late afternoon.
The church is a place of worship, so dress with shoulders and knees covered and stay quiet during Mass.
For exterior photos, the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low, is best.
Check posted Mass times and event schedules locally. You can ask at the parish office.
Combining Calape with Loon Church makes for an efficient day.
Tell the conductor on the bus that you are getting off at "Calape Church."
Bring enough cash. Many small-town places do not accept cards.
Check the weather and boats first before visiting an island.
Check the last bus or van time for the return trip in advance.
The outline of the façade matters, so first look at the whole from across the plaza, and then go closer to examine the portico and the belfry decoration; this makes it easier to understand.
The church is a working parish, so viewing may be restricted during Mass and events. Check local notices for opening hours and interior rules.
Bus fares (about ₱80~170) vary widely by source, so confirm when boarding, and check van and tricycle fares locally.
Showers are frequent on rainy days, so bring an umbrella.
Boats to the islands can be canceled depending on the weather.
We could not confirm whether the bell tower can be climbed, so do not go up without permission.
